newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle crew prepares for satellite pickup.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle crew prepares for satellite pickup.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Columbia prepared to pick up a prototype space factory about three hours earlier than planned on Monday.
Retrieval of the Wake Shield Facility was moved up so the Orfeus-Spas telescope, an orbiting observatory also deployed by Columbia, would not stray too close to it, NASA officials said.
"We're looking forward to a good rendezvous today," mission control's Bill McArthur said.
When the astronauts woke up, they were 23 miles (36.8 km) ahead of the Wake Shield, the experimental factory released by Columbia on Friday night.

Blaring out the pop song "Let the Good Times Roll" by The Cars, mission control woke up the five astronauts one hour earlier so they could begin steering the spacecraft for the interception, now scheduled for 8:56 p.m EST (0156 GMT).

Mission control congratulated astronaut Story Musgrave on exceeding 1,000 hours in space. Musgrave, 61, is the oldest person to fly in space and was making his sixth, and most likely last, shuttle flight.
"Story is looking marvellous for a 1,001-hour space traveller," Shuttle Commander Ken Cockrell, 46, said.
"We just made a beautiful pass over Hawaii. The islands are clear today. No matter how many hours you've got up here, these ones are just as good as the first ones," Musgrave said.
Later on Monday afternoon, astronaut Tom Jones, 41, was to activate the shuttle's 50-foot long robot arm which he will use to grab the Wake Shield.

The space factory and telescope are expected to be 13 miles (20.8 km) apart when Columbia swoops in to collect the Wake Shield. The craft must be separated by at least 12.5 miles (20 km) for a safe retrieval, shuttle flight director Rob Kelso said.
The telescope ceased observations on Sunday afternoon so it could be turned to reduce the atmosphere's braking effect.

NASA believes the two craft drew unexpectedly close when the Orfeus-Spas telescope encountered more drag than expected from the thin upper atmosphere 220 miles (355 km) up as it was pointed at its celestial targets. The telescope resumed its activities at about 5 a.m. EST (1000 GMT) on Monday.

The saucer-shaped Wake Shield was designed to manufacture ultra-pure semiconductors for the electronics industry. They could lead to faster computer chips and better, smaller cellular phones. NASA officials said they were very pleased with the performance of the space factory during the three days it spent orbiting apart from Columbia.
It is the first time NASA has flown the shuttle in formation with two recoverable satellites. Flight director Al Pennington said before the mission the task would be "tricky."
The decision not to retrieve the Wake Shield a day early allowed it to complete its seventh and final semiconductor manufacturing run.
The five astronauts, who are more than one-third of the way through a 16-day mission, took six hours off duty on Sunday and made private phone calls to their families.
